h: Getting the Most From Kite Hour
p: The magic at Gigrin happens in a rush, so the trick is to be settled before the first kite drops. Get to the hides in good time, pick your spot, and let the kids get the fidgets out before the food goes down. Once it starts, the sky can go from a handful of birds to a whirling crowd in what feels like seconds, and you don't want to be fumbling with your coat buttons when it does.

If you're taking photos, a fast shutter speed is your best friend, because kites twist and stall in a way that blurs easily. Burst mode on a phone helps too. Don't spend the whole time behind a screen, though; some of the best moments are simply watching a bird snatch food mid-air with that flick of the forked tail and hearing the gasps from everyone around you. Binoculars are handy for picking out the buzzards and ravens loitering at the edges of the action, waiting for their chance.

Winter is a cracking time to go, as natural food is scarcer and the birds can gather in big numbers, but the show runs through the year. Dress as though you're standing still on a Welsh hillside, because that's exactly what you'll be doing.

Rhayader sits on the River Wye, and its Welsh name, Rhaeadr Gwy, means waterfall on the Wye, a nod to the falls that once tumbled through the town before the bridge was built. It's a handy stop on the A470 if you're crossing Wales north to south, with cafés, pubs and outdoor shops for anything you forgot. Stay late on a clear night and the Elan Valley's status as an International Dark Sky Park means the stars put on a show almost as good as the kites.
